title: Walking in
hookLine: behind a screen or face to face; bless me Father, it's been this long
carry: the hardest part is the door

lines: A LIGHT ABOVE A WOODEN DOOR.
cards: Saturday afternoon, a side aisle of a parish church. Five people sit in a pew near a wooden door with a little light above it. When the light goes off, the next one gets up.
You can tell who hasn't been in years: they're reading a card from the pamphlet rack, lips moving, and when it's their turn they stand up like someone going in for a job interview.
Ask a priest who hears confessions and he may tell you the hardest part isn't what's said inside. It's the walk from the pew to the door.

teach.h: NO BOX FOR MOST OF HISTORY.
teach.b: First, the room. For long stretches of Church history there was no box.

teach.h: BEHIND A SCREEN, OR FACE TO FACE.
teach.b: People confessed face to face, often kneeling beside the priest.
Historians link the wooden confessional with a screen to the years after the Council of Trent, and to Charles Borromeo, archbishop of Milan, who promoted it to protect privacy and dignity.
Today many parishes offer both: kneel behind the screen and stay anonymous, or sit in a chair across from the priest. Your choice; nobody minds which. Then, the words.

teach.h: BLESS ME, FATHER, FOR I HAVE SINNED.
teach.b: The traditional opening is: Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. Then you say how long it's been since your last confession. A week.
Two years. Twenty-five years. Priests hear every answer, and a long time is not a scandal; it's a return.
If you've forgotten what to do, just say so. The priest will walk you through it; that's part of his job.

Then you say your sins simply, without a speech. Serious ones should be named with roughly how often; you don't need the whole backstory. The priest may give a few words of advice, or a short line of Scripture.
After that come a prayer of sorrow, a penance, and the words of absolution, which are the next two days.
And if you truly can't remember something, the Church teaches it's forgiven along with the rest, as long as it wasn't hidden on purpose. The whole thing is often over in a few minutes.

teach.h: THE HARDEST PART IS THE DOOR.
teach.b: The door is the hard part.

how: Catholics go to confession at set parish times, often Saturday afternoons, choosing to kneel behind a screen or sit face to face, and usually begin by saying how long it has been since their last confession.

o: the procession up the aisle at the start of Mass
entering a church for Sunday Mass after a long time
going into confession, behind a screen or face to face

games.q: what's inside the confessional — tap the pairs.

s: confessionals have been in churches since the beginning
historians link the screened confessional to the years after the Council of Trent.
you must confess face to face
many parishes offer both a screen and a face-to-face chair.
if you've forgotten how, you can tell the priest

games.q: it's your turn. you haven't been in fifteen years and you've forgotten everything. what do you do?
o: leave the line before anyone notices.
go in and say it's been fifteen years and you've forgotten how.
wait until you've memorized it all.
games.why: priests hear it all the time. a long time away is a return, not a scandal, and he'll guide you.

practice: If you're Catholic, say the opening words quietly to yourself: Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been, and then however long it's really been.
If you're not Catholic, picture a door you've been avoiding, an apology, a doctor's appointment, a conversation, and see yourself walk up to it, stand there, and open it.

wordCard.voice: Walking in. Behind a screen or face to face, with the old opening words, bless me, Father, and however long it's been. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the hardest part is the door. A long time away is a return, not a scandal. See you tomorrow.
